title: Serum taurine affects lung cancer progression by regulating tumor immune escape mediated by the immune microenvironment

sections.introduction:
Lung cancer, with its extremely low 5-year survival rate, is recognized as the most mortal cancer all over the world [1] . In 2023 and 2024, lung cancer accounted for over 20 % of cancer-related deaths in the United States [2] , [3] . Likewise, in China, morbidity and mortality of lung cancer has been increasing for the past few decades [4] . The main reason for this phenomenon is lack of in-depth knowledge of carcinogenesis and deficiency of precise diagnostic methods at earlier stages [5] , [6] . It’s time for us to pay more attention to the initialization and progression of cancer cells [4] . Among all the factors, tumor metabolomics plays an important role in the tumorigenesis and tumor progression [7] . Thus, it has been practiced in diagnosis and treatment of different cancers. However, as cellular metabolic processes contain abundant information, the pathogenetic role of them in cancer is still mystery [7] , [8] . In general, tumor metabolites including glucose, amino acid, and lipids metabolism. It has been proved that actate, pyruvate, and fatty acids are up-regulated in tumor cells than normal cells, for the reason that tumor cells need higher rates of catabolite uptake, transfer, and utilization [9] , [10] . Moreover, tumor metabolic ecology enables constituent cells to produce ATP, maintain redox balance, and perform biosynthesis, thereby supporting tumorigenesis and tumor progression [10] .

Taurine is a special amino acid with high concentrations in many cells [11] and also a kind of conditionally essential nutrient in humans [12] . As an important metabolite, taurine plays an important part in bile salt coupling, osmotic regulation, membrane stabilization, calcium regulation, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory and is utilized in the treatment of congestive heart failure, liver disease and stroke-like seizures [13] , [14] , [15] , [16] , [17] . Besides, taurine is also playing an increasingly important role in suppressing cancer progression. Taurine is reported to have mesenchymal transition (EMT) inhibitory effects on human prostate cancer cells by down-regulating the expression of N-cadherin, TWIST1, ZEB1, SNAIL, vimentin and increasing E-cadherin expression [18] . Taurine can also attenuate cancer cells metastasis probably by regulating oxidant/anti-oxidant responses, decreasing the levels of angiogenic markers and inducing matrix remodelling [19] . Thanks to the ability to predicting the tumor malignant transformation and formation, taurine obviously suppresses the potential proliferation, invasion and metastasis for breast, bladder and colorectal cancer [11] , [20] .

Our exploration of the role of taurine, a crucial metabolite, in the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of cancers has unveiled some intriguing findings. Our previous study discovered that taurine had high abundance in plasma of 110 Chinese patients with lung cancer compared to healthy individuals [21] . Similarly, high abundance of taurine in plasma was also found in the established lung cancer mouse model platform, which seemed to be a bad omen [22] . Despite these compelling associations, the precise impact and mechanism of elevated serum taurine levels on lung cancer progression remain unclear. It is necessary to fully understand the role and regulatory mechanism of taurine on lung tumor growth. Consequently, our study set out to systematically investigate the role of taurine in lung cancer, with the ultimate goal of contributing novel strategies for lung cancer treatment.
sections.methods:
Mouse Lewis lung carcinoma (LLC) and A549 cells (ATCC: Manassas, VA, USA) were cultured in RPMI DMEM or 1640 containing 10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS, Origin: Canada), 50 µg/ml penicillin and 50 µg/ml streptomycin (Thermo Scientific: San Diego, CA, USA). Cells were maintained at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere with 5 % CO 2 .

All designed animal experiments were based on committee-approved protocols and institutional animal care guidelines (Registration number: A014/DICV/DIS/2019, Date: 29/8/2019). All collected NSCLC samples were obtained with patients’ informed consent and approved by the ethics committee of Hubei Taihe Hospital.

To establish LLC subcutaneously, 5 × 10 5 LLC cells were suspended in 100 μl free FBS RPMI DMEM medium. Then mice were injected subcutaneously into the right flank of female C57BL/6 mice (C57, 6–8 weeks) with sterile syringes (1 cc/ml, U-40, 0.40 mm × 13 mm, Terumo Corporation). When LLC-xenografted tumor were reached a size around 30 mm 3 (on the seventh day), mice could be randomly divided into the model group ( n = 6), taurine (purity > 98 %, CAS NO.107–35-7: Dalian Meilun Biological Technology Co., Ltd., China.) at different doses (25 mg/kg, 50 mg/kg, 100 mg/kg, 200 mg/kg, and 400 mg/kg, i.p., n = 6 per group), and taurine beverage (0.4 ml/20 g, p.o., n = 6). Mice received repeated treatments with PBS, different doses of taurine or taurine beverage every day. The electronic balance and caliper were applied to measure the body weight and tumor volume of mice every three days.

The ROS concentrations in plasma of seven groups including C57 mice-taurine low ( n = 3), C57 mice-taurine high ( n = 3), C57 mice-model ( n = 3), C57 mice-control ( n = 3), nude mice-taurine low ( n = 3) nude mice-model ( n = 3) and nude mice-control ( n = 3) were tested by mouse reactive oxygen species (ROS) ELISA Kit (SANCHAI KESHUN SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOY CO., LTD, Cat: KS19189). Before detection, the whole blood of mice was thoroughly mixed with heparin sodium, and the supernatant was obtained as the plasma sample by centrifugation at 3000 rpm for 10 min.

In this study, the fluorochrome-conjugated anti-mouse CD3-APC (BioLegend, Cat: 100235), CD4-FITC (BioLegend, Cat: 100406), CD8-PE/Cy7 (BioLegend, Cat: 980910), PD-1-PE (BioLegend, Cat: 135224), and CD45-Percp (BioLegend, Cat: 103130) antibody were used to stain single-cell suspensions. Data in peripheral blood from model, taurine low (25 mg/kg) and taurine high (200 mg/kg) groups were collected with a BD Aria III Flow Cytometer (BD Biosciences, San Jose, California, USA) and analyzed with FlowJo Software. Expression of programmed death-1 (PD-1) was investigated both on CD4 and CD8 T cells.

Total RNA was extracted from 15 tumor samples divided into five experimental groups: C57 mice with low taurine (n = 3), C57 mice with high taurine (n = 3), C57 model mice (n = 3), nude mice with low taurine (n = 3), and nude model mice (n = 3). The extraction was performed using Trizol reagent, adhering strictly to the manufacturer's protocol to ensure consistency and reliability in RNA yield and purity. The quality and purity of the extracted RNA were evaluated using the Bioanalyzer 2100 and RNA 6000 Nano LabChip Kit. Only samples with a RNA Integrity Number (RIN) greater than 7.0 were selected for subsequent library construction. This quality control measure was crucial to minimize variability and ensure the integrity of the sequencing data. Following RNA extraction, mRNA was isolated from the total RNA using Dynabeads Oligo (dT) through two rounds of purification. This step enriched the mRNA fraction, which is essential for subsequent transcriptome analysis. The purified mRNA was fragmented into short pieces using divalent cations at elevated temperatures. Specifically, the Magnesium RNA Fragmentation Module was used under controlled conditions (94 °C for 5–7 min) to achieve the desired fragment size suitable for downstream applications. The fragmented RNA was reverse-transcribed into complementary DNA (cDNA) using SuperScript™ II Reverse Transcriptase. Subsequently, second-strand cDNA synthesis was performed with uracil (U) labeling, employing E. coli DNA polymerase I, RNase H, and dUTP Solution. This process ensured accurate synthesis and labeling of the cDNA, facilitating subsequent steps in the sequencing workflow. An adenine (A) base was added to the blunt ends of each cDNA strand to prepare them for adapter ligation. Indexed adapters with a thymine (T) overhang were ligated to the cDNA fragments. Size selection was then performed using AMPureXP beads, targeting fragments of approximately 300 ± 50 base pairs. This step was critical for generating high-quality sequencing libraries. The ligated cDNA products were amplified via polymerase chain reaction (PCR) under the following conditions: initial denaturation at 95 °C for 3 min, followed by 8 cycles of denaturation at 98 °C for 15 s, annealing at 60 °C for 15 s, and extension at 72 °C for 30 s, with a final extension at 72 °C for 5 min. This amplification ensured sufficient cDNA yield for sequencing. The prepared cDNA libraries underwent 2 × 150 bp paired-end sequencing on an Illumina Novaseq™ 6000 platform, following the manufacturer's recommended protocol. This high-throughput sequencing approach provided comprehensive transcriptomic data, enabling a detailed analysis of the effects of taurine treatment in different mouse models.

Initially, RNA-Seq reads were assembled into transcripts using StringTie (version 1.3.4d) with default parameters, ensuring a reliable foundation for subsequent analysis. These assembled transcriptomes from all samples were then integrated into a comprehensive transcriptome using gffcompare (version 0.9.8), which aligns and consolidates transcript predictions to capture transcriptomic diversity. Following this, StringTie and ballgown were employed to estimate transcript abundance and explore expression data, respectively. Expression levels were normalized using the FPKM metric, allowing for accurate cross-sample comparisons. The workflow, combining StringTie for assembly and quantification, gffcompare for merging, and ballgown for statistical analysis, proved effective in capturing and quantifying transcriptomic data, providing a robust framework for understanding gene expression and supporting further genomic research [23] , [24] .

Differential expression analysis of genes was conducted using DESeq2 for comparisons between distinct groups and edgeR for comparisons between individual samples. Genes meeting the criteria of a false discovery rate (FDR) below 0.05 and an absolute fold change of ≥2 were identified as differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Subsequently, the DEGs underwent enrichment analysis to elucidate their functional implications using Gene Ontology (GO) for biological processes, molecular functions, and cellular components, as well as Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways [25] , [26] , [27] .

Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was performed using GSEA software (v4.1.0) and MSigDB to assess differential enrichment of gene sets associated with specific GO terms and KEGG pathways between distinct groups. The analysis involved inputting the gene expression matrix and ranking genes via the Signal2Noise normalization method. Enrichment scores and statistical significance were calculated using default parameters. GO terms and KEGG pathways meeting criteria of |NES|>1 (Normalized Enrichment Score), NOM p-val < 0.05 (nominal p-value), and FDR q-val < 0.25 (False Discovery Rate q-value) were considered significantly differentially enriched between the groups. This approach facilitated the identification of biological processes and pathways exhibiting substantial differences in gene expression patterns, thereby providing critical insights into the functional distinctions between the compared groups [28] , [29] .

The RNA-seq dataset comprises 1017 samples from patients diagnosed with lung cancer, including both lung adenocarcinoma and lung squamous carcinoma subtypes. These samples were retrieved from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) repository and accessed through the UCSC Xena database ( https://xenabrowser.net/datapages/ ). This extensive dataset serves as a crucial resource for studying gene expression profiles across diverse lung cancer types, enabling in-depth molecular analyses and comparative investigations within the field. The correlation between Nfe2l1 and key genes of the taurine metabolism pathway was calculated. Spearman correlation analyses were performed between Nfe2l1 expression and key genes expression of the taurine metabolism pathway. |r| > 0.1 and p < 0.05 were set as the criteria for the significant correlation. Then, the ggplot2 package in R software was used to construct correlation scatter plots [29] , [30] .

The detailed procedure was reported previously [31] . The following antibodies were used in this experiment: β-Actin (CST#8457), Nfe2l1 (Nrf1, SANTA: sc-28379), 41BBL (CD137L, SANTA: sc-398933), PD-1 (CST#84651), NF-κB (CST#8242), and p-NF-κB (CST#3033). Amersham ImageQuant™ 800 Western blot imaging systems was used to quantify the signal intensity (Cytiva, Japan).

In this study, 1.5 × 10 6 (for nude mice) or 5 × 10 5 (for C57 mice) LLC cells were suspended in 100 μl free FBS medium and then injected subcutaneously into the right flank of balb/c female nude mice (6–8 weeks) or C57 female mice (6–8 weeks). On the seventh day following xenograft implantation, when tumors had reached approximately 30 mm 3 in size, mice were randomly allocated to experimental groups and received repeated treatments with vehicle 1 (PBS, i.p. or p.o., experiment 1, n = 4), taurine (25 mg/kg, i.p., experiment 1, n = 4), vehicle 2 (PBS, p.o., experiment 2, n ≥ 4), taurine beverage (0.4 ml/20 g, p.o., experiment 2, n ≥ 4), vehicle 3 (PBS, p.o., experiment 3, n ≥ 4), taurine (25 mg/kg, i.p., experiment 3, n ≥ 4), taurine (75 mg/kg, p.o., experiment 3, n ≥ 4), or taurine (75 mg/kg, p.o., experiment 3) combined with cholic acid (purity > 98.5 %, CAS NO. 81-25-4, MedChemExpress) at a dose of 245.25 mg/kg ( p.o., experiment 3, n ≥ 4) every day. The electronic balance and caliper were applied to measure the body weight and tumor volume of mice every three days.

About 5 × 10 6 A549 cells were suspended in 100 μl free FBS 1640 medium and then injected subcutaneously into the right flank of balb/c female nude mice (6–8 weeks). On the seventh day post-xenograft implantation, when tumors had grown to approximately 50 mm 3 in size, mice were randomly assigned to two experimental groups: the model group (n = 5) and the taurine group (n = 5). The mice received intraperitoneal injections of either vehicle (PBS) or taurine at a dose of 25 mg/kg every three days. Throughout the experimental period, the weights of the mice and the sizes of their tumors were measured every third day using an electronic balance and caliper, respectively.

A Lentiviral overexpression vector expressing mouse Nfe2l1 gene was constructed under the control of EFS promoter. The Lentiviral was packaged with the overexpressed vector and tested for titer to ensure that the quality of the virus met the requirements of follow-up experiments. For cell screen, it was necessarily to screened the bacteria, fungus, mycoplasma, and others to ensure no pollution for LLC cells. Then cells were transduced by Lentivirus, and the resistant cells were selected with corresponding antibiotics to obtain stable cell lines including mouse Nfe2l1 overexpression stable cell lines and the control virus transfected cell lines. At last, quantitative RT-PCR was applied to detect mouse Nfe2l1 expression on overexpression stably strain and control cell lines.

LLC cells were treated with taurine at various concentrations (0, 1, 10, 100, and 1000 μM) for approximately 24 h, 48 h and 72 h. Total RNA was then extracted using TRIzol reagent. After reverse transcription of RNA into cDNA, quantitative real-time PCR was performed using the ViiA™ 7 system. Gene expression levels were calculated using the 2 −△△Ct method. Primers were obtained from Sangon Biotech (Shanghai) and their sequences are provided in Table S1 .

LLC (wt, 1000 cells/well) and LLC ( Nfe2l1 overexpression, 1000 cells/well) cells were seeded in 96-well microplates. Cells were in an incubator at 37 °C for 72 h after adhesion. Then 10 μl MTT solution (0.5 mg/ml) was added into each well and microplates were placed in an incubator at 37 °C for 4 h. Then DMSO (100 μl/well) was added to melt the crystals. Absorbance was recorded with spectrometer at 570 and 650 nm.

LLC (wt, 3 × 10 4 cells/well) and LLC ( Nfe2l1 overexpression, 3 × 10 4 cells/well) cells were seeded in a 6-well plate. Cells were in an incubator at 37 °C separately for approximately 72 h after adhesion. 4 % paraformaldehyde (PFA) was added in each well for 30 min at 4 °C when colonies were significantly formed. Then crystal violet solution was used for cell staining for at least thirty minutes. After washing away the crystal violet solution, colonies were photographed.

Human tissue of NSCLC patients derived from 2014 to 2017 were collected in Taihe Hospital [31] . Immunohistochemistry (IHC) analyses were conducted utilizing the DAKO EnVision system, following protocols previously established in the literature. The primary antibody employed for these analyses was Nfe2l1 (Nrf1, catalog number sc-28379, Santa Cruz Biotechnology). This investigation, involving patients with NSCLC, received ethical approval from the Hubei Taihe Hospital Ethics Committee.

All data are reported as the mean ± standard deviation (SD) or the mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Statistical significance was evaluated using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by post hoc t-tests, conducted with GraphPad Prism 7 software (San Diego, CA, USA). A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered indicative of statistical significance.
sections.results:
Our recent work has documented taurine’s dual role in lung cancer progression in immune-competent mice. Here, we report that low doses of taurine (25 and 50 mg/kg), as well as taurine-infused beverages at equivalent doses, significantly enhance LLC-xenografted tumor growth ( Fig. 1 A-E and Supplementary Fig. S1-S2 ). Equally intriguing is the observation that the promoting effect of taurine on lung cancer progression wanes as the dosage increases. Specifically, taurine at 100 mg/kg has no significant impact on lung cancer progression, while higher doses (200 and 400 mg/kg) actively inhibit lung cancer growth. Moreover, high doses of taurine (100–400 mg/kg) can cause a decrease in liver/body ratio, indicating a risk of liver damage ( Fig. 1 F, Supplementary Fig. S2 F). Besides, taurine (400 mg/kg) can also cause a decrease in mouse body weight, indicating the potential toxicity effects of high dose taurine on mice ( Supplementary Fig. S2 B). Fig. 1 Taurine demonstrates a dual role in lung cancer progression in immune-competent mice. (A) Experimental flow chart of taurine’s dual effect on lung cancer progression in vivo ( n = 6). (B-C) Body weight and tumor volumes of mice were examined every three days. (D) After dissection, tumor size was significantly reduced or increased in different doses of taurine or taurine beverage (0.4 ml/20 g, p.o.) groups compared to the control group according to representative images of tumors from C57 mice. (E-F) Weights of tumors and organ/body ratios were measured and calculated. (G) Taurine significantly regulated plasma ROS levels in C57 mice but not in nude mice ( n = 3). (H) Different taurine doses led to differences in PD-1 levels in both CD4 + and CD8 + T cells ( n = 4). Statistical significance was calculated by means of ANOVA analysis. All data are presented as the mean ± SEM, * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, and *** p < 0.001.

Up-regulated ROS are well-recognized for their level dependent roles in cancer proliferation [32] . ROS demonstrate a ‘double-edged sword’ activity in tumor cells [32] , [33] , where an appropriate concentration of ROS promotes tumor cell proliferation, while an excess of ROS can induce tumor cell death through various pathways. Our results mirror this duality, with different taurine doses, especially taurine at 200 mg/kg, significantly elevating ROS levels in plasma of mice ( Fig. 1 G). Mechanistically, low dose of taurine significantly elevated PD-1 levels on CD4 + and CD8 + T cells in the peripheral blood of C57BL/6 (C57) mice ( Fig. 1 H and Supplementary Fig. S3-S5 ). Simultaneously, the up-regulation of PD-1 levels induced by taurine diminishes with increasing dosage.

To dissect the regulatory mechanisms of taurinés influence on tumor growth, we employed RNA sequencing on lung tumors ( Supplementary Fig. S6-S8 ). We then performed GSEA enrichment analysis to further explore the biological pathways and functions of genes across the model group, taurine 25 mg/kg group, and taurine 200 mg/kg group. The results of GSEA-GO analysis indicated that gene sets related to “peroxidase activity” and “cellular oxidant detoxification” were significantly enriched in model group, while their enrichment was lower in taurine 25 mg/kg group ( Fig. 2 A-F). Instead, gene sets related to immune system functions, such as “adaptive immune response” and “immune system process” ( p < 0.001), were significantly enriched in taurine 25 mg/kg group, but were less pronounced in model group. Similarly, GSEA-KEGG analysis results showed that gene sets related to immune response pathways, such as “Th1 and Th2 cell differentiation” and “cAMP signaling pathway” ( p < 0.001), were significantly enriched in taurine 25 mg/kg group, but were less pronounced in model group ( Fig. 2 G-L). In the GSEA-GO ( Supplementary Fig. S9 A-F) and GSEA-KEGG ( Supplementary Fig. S9 G-L) analyses, gene sets related to functions and pathways of antitumor immunity in the tumor microenvironment were enriched in taurine 200 mg/kg group ( p < 0.05, p < 0.01, or p < 0.001). This indicated that there were differences in the expression patterns of genes related to biological functions of immune response and oxidative stress across the model group, taurine 25 mg/kg group, and taurine 200 mg/kg group. Moreover, GO enrichment ( Fig. 3 A and Supplementary Fig. S10 ), and KEGG ( Supplementary Fig. S11 ) analyses, further reveal the pivotal roles played by immune response and oxidative stress in mediating taurine's differential effects on lung tumor growth. Fig. 2 The promoting effect of low-dose taurine on lung cancer progression is related to the up-regulation of oxidative stress functions and the down-regulation of immune response functions. (G-L) Gene sets related to immune response pathways were significantly enriched in taurine 25 mg/kg group, but were less pronounced in model group. Nfe2l1 is implicated in both oxidative stress and immune response [34] , [35] , indicating its critical role in the regulatory mechanisms of taurine on tumor growth. Among the top 100 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with biological significance ( Fig. 3 B), we identified 7 DEGs that exhibited distinct responses to varying taurine doses (25 and 200 mg/kg) in comparison to the model groups ( Fig. 3 C). Notably, Nfe2l1 displayed the highest expression abundance based on FPKM values. Correspondingly, low-dose taurine significantly down-regulated Nfe2l1 levels, while high-dose taurine yielded the opposite results. In addition, reduced Nfe2l1 expression is a common feature in many cancers and associated with poor prognosis in some cases, as observed in the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) data ( Supplementary Fig. S12-S13 ). Moreover, Nfe2l1 significantly up-regulates ROS levels by activating tumor necrosis factor ligand superfamily member 9 (41BBL), thereby inducing tumor immune response and ultimately inhibiting tumor growth [36] . We found that high doses of taurine up-regulated Nfe2l1 and 41BBL protein levels and down-regulated PD-1 protein levels ( Fig. 3 D). Interestingly, overexpressed Nfe2l1 significantly inhibited lung cancer progression, along with the up-regulation of 41BBL protein levels ( Fig. 3 E-J and Supplementary Fig. S14 ). Consequently, the Nfe2l1/41BBL axis emerges as a vital mediator in the interplay between oxidative stress and tumor immune response.

Taurine is one of the most abundant amino acids in many cells and synthesized mainly through taurine and hypotaurine metabolism in vivo [22] , [37] . Spearman correlation analyses were performed to further verify the correlation between Nfe2l1 expression and taurine metabolism pathway. In our results, Nfe2l1 expression was significantly correlated with key targets in the taurine metabolism pathway, including Cysteine Sulfinic Acid Decarboxylase (CSAD), 2-aminoethanethiol Dioxygenase (ADO), Gamma-glutamyltransferase 6 (GGT6), Gamma-glutamyltransferase 7 (GGT7), Flavin Containing Dimethylaniline Monoxygenase 1 (FMO1), Glutamate Decarboxylase 1 (GAD1), Bile Acid-CoA: Amino Acid N-Acyltransferase (BAAT), and Cysteine Dioxygenase Type 1 (CDO1) ( Fig. 4 A-H and Supplementary Fig. S15 ). Therefore, the results further validate the highly significant correlation between Nfe2l1 expression and the taurine metabolism pathway. Fig. 4 Nfe2l1 is highly significantly correlated with key targets of taurine metabolism pathway. (A-H) Nfe2l1 was significantly correlated with key targets in the taurine metabolism pathway, including CSAD, ADO, GGT6, GGT7, FMO1, GAD1, BAAT, and. CDO1. Spearman correlation analysis was applied to analyse the correlation between Nfe2l1 and the taurine metabolism pathway in 1017 lung cancer samples (including lung adenocarcinoma and lung squamous cell carcinoma) from the TCGA data.

To further validate the role of taurine in lung cancer progression, we established Lewis lung carcinoma (LLC)-xenografted lung cancer models in both immune-competent and immune-deficient mouse strains. We found opposing effects of taurine on tumor growth depending on immune competence ( Fig. 5 A-G and Supplementary Fig. S16-S22 ). In C57 mice, taurine significantly boosted lung tumor growth. However, in nude mice, taurine markedly inhibited tumor growth, aligning with reported results [20] . Furthermore, taurine at 25 mg/kg significantly inhibited A549-xenografted tumor growth in nude mice ( Supplementary Fig. S18 ). Fig. 5 Immune competence determines taurine's impacts on lung cancer progression. (A) Diagram of taurine showing opposite results in lung cancer progression in C57 and nude mice. (B) Taurine potentially promoted lung tumor growth in C57 mice ( n = 4). (C) Conversely, taurine with the same dose potentially inhibited lung tumor growth in nude mice ( n = 4). (D) Taurine beverage similarly accelerated lung cancer progression in C57 mice ( n = 6). (E) However, taurine beverage revealed anti-lung tumor effects in nude mice ( n = 4). (F) The tumor-promoting effects of taurine could be reversed by bile acids in C57 mice ( n = 6). (G) Similarly, the anti-tumor effects of taurine could also be reversed by bile acids in nude mice ( n = 4). Statistical significance was calculated by means of ANOVA analysis. All data are presented as the mean ± SEM, * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, and *** p < 0.001.

All data are presented as the mean ± SEM, * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, and *** p < 0.001.

Functional beverages are products which claim a health benefit and contain nontraditional ingredients like minerals, vitamins, specific amino acids, dietary fibers, or probiotics [38] . Given the varying concentrations of taurine found in functional beverages, we assessed the effects of a popular functional drink available on the market. Intriguingly, consumption of the taurine beverage had opposite effects on tumor growth in C57 ( Fig. 5 D and Supplementary Fig. S19 ) and nude mice ( Fig. 5 E and Supplementary Fig. S20 ).

Bile acids, especially cholic acid, ursodeoxycholic acid, and chenodeoxycholic acid, can form conjugates with taurine as taurine scavengers [39] , [40] . Interestingly, the tumor-promoting effect induced by taurine could be mitigated by cholic acid in C57 mice ( Fig. 5 F and Supplementary Fig. S21 ). Similarly, the anti-tumor effect induced by taurine was neutralized by cholic acid in nude mice ( Fig. 5 G and Supplementary Fig. S22 ). Consequently, cholic acid could potentially act as an effective agent for scavenging taurine and reversing its effects. Additionally, other medicinal bile acids may also hold promise as effective therapeutic agents.

Interestingly, taurine failed up-regulating ROS levels in nude mice ( Fig. 6 A). We postulate that taurine might inhibit tumor growth through pathways distinct from regulating ROS levels in nude mice. Our GO enrichment analysis highlights a strong correlation between the anti-tumor effects and NF-κB-mediated inflammation in nude mice ( Fig. 6 B). Then, we identified 4 DEGs including angiotensin converting enzyme ( Ace ), Placenta-specific 8 ( Plac8 ), Guanylate-binding protein 4 ( Gbp4 ), and Nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-containing protein 1 ( Nod1 ) by comparing the gene expression profiles of tumors among two groups ( Fig. 6 C-D). In the result, the 4 DEGs were significantly up-regulated by taurine in nude mice. To validate whether our findings met the clinical significance, we examined expression of Ace , Plac8 , Gbp4 and Nod1 in a human lung cancer transcriptome dataset from TCGA. Consistent with our findings, the 4 DEGs are down-regulated in both lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) tumors compared with normal lung tissues ( Supplementary Fig. S23 ). Moreover, the 4 DEGs were reported to be closely related to inflammation and apoptosis and applied to cancer therapy [41] , [42] , [43] , [44] . Notably, taurine down-regulated p-NF-κB protein in nude mice, but not in C57 mice ( Fig. 6 E-F). Therefore, taurine may exert anti-tumor effects by inhibiting NF-κB-mediated inflammatory responses in nude mice. However, our in vitro experiments revealed that taurine alone did not significantly affect Nfe2l1 gene expression in LLC cells ( Supplementary Fig. S24 ). We also investigated the regulatory effect of taurine on Nfe2l1 level in nude mice. In our results, taurine did not affect Nfe2l1 protein levels in nude mice. And interestingly enough, overexpressed Nfe2l1 also failed inhibiting tumor growth in nude mice ( Fig. 6 G-K), implying that Nfe2l1 exhibits anti-tumor effects only in immune-competent mice. Furthermore, Nfe2l1 gene ( Fig. 7 A) and protein ( Fig. 7 B-D) were down-regulated in young lung cancer patients. As patients age increased, Nfe2l1 gradually returned to the levels observed in healthy individuals. However, high expression of Nfe2l1 failed significantly improving the survival of lung cancer patients ( Fig. 7 E). sections.discussion:
As an important metabolite, taurine has the potential to predict tumor malignant transformation and formation. It has been documented that taurine plays an important role in inhibiting the development of cancer. Taurine is capable of suppressing EMT of human prostate cancer cells by down-regulating the expression of N-cadherin, TWIST1, ZEB1, SNAIL, vimentin and increasing E-cadherin expression [18] . Taurine also potentially inhibits cancer cells metastasis by regulating oxidant/anti-oxidant responses, decreasing the levels of angiogenic markers and inducing matrix remodelling [19] . taurine also has the potential to suppress the potential proliferation, invasion and metastasis for breast, bladder and colorectal cancer [11] , [20] . Moreover, in lung cancer, taurine can significantly suppress tumor proliferation by upregulating the expression of p53 upregulated modulator of apoptosis and Bax, downregulating the Bcl‑2 expression, and increasing the ratio of Bax/Bcl‑2 [45] . Similarly, in our results, taurine can significantly suppress tumor growth in nude mice ( Fig. 6 C, E, G). Moreover, in C57 mice, high dose of taurine (200 and 400 mg/kg) also revealed obvious anti-tumor effect on lung cancer ( Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. S2 ).

However, there are only few indirect evidences about the promoting effects of taurine on cancer progression. Taurine transporte, a target gene of p53 tumor suppressor, is reported to promote tumor growth. Knockdown of TauT can block taurine uptake by tumor cells and selectively lead to tumor cells death, which indirectly suggests the tumor-promoting effect of taurine [46] . At present, there are still no direct reports on the tumor-promoting effect of taurine. To our surprise, we found that low dose of taurine (25 and 50 mg/kg) significant promoted lung tumor growth in C57 mice ( Fig. 1 ). Therefore, the promoting effect of low-dose taurine on lung cancer progression was the first discovery of our study.

Nfe2l1 is reported to be capable of inhibiting the carcinogenic process and impacting chemosensitivity [47] . Consistent with reported results, the low dose of taurine can significantly promote tumor growth with the down-regulated expression of Nfe2l1 while high dose of taurine can significantly inhibit tumor growth and up-regulate the expression of Nfe2l1 . Furthermore, Nfe2l1 is reported to participate in both oxidative stress [48] and immune response [36] , which was also proved by our RNA sequencing finding. Firstly, Nfe2l1 plays a vital role in regulating the cellular antioxidant response especially ROS level [48] . ROS, generated mainly through the mitochondrial electron transport chain and tricarboxylic acid cycle, plays a dual role in cancer therapy [32] . Excess ROS can escape immune surveillance and immune defense and induce tumor-promoting effects by suppressing the functiong of T cells and NK cells, facilitating the recruitment and M2 polarization for macrophage, and activating EMT in cancer cell [32] , [33] . However, the massive accumulation of ROS can inhibit tumor growth by blocking cancer cell proliferation including blocking proliferation signaling pathway, arresting cell cycle and inhibiting the biosynthesis of nucleotides and ATP [32] , [33] . For this reason, we tested the ROS level in plasma of immune-deficiency/competent mice treated with taurine. Consistent with the reported results, low dose of taurine (25 mg/kg) can significantly increase ROS level compared to control group rather than model group, indicating that low dose of taurine can promote tumor growth by induce excess ROS ( Fig. 1 G). On the contrary, the ROS level in taurine high group (200 mg/kg) was both higher than that in the control and model group. Therefore, taurine may play a dual role in tumor growth probably by regulating ROS level.

41BBL is reported to bind to 41BB to form 41BB/41BBL complex [36] . The complex, expressing on activated T lymphocytes, can discover cancer immunotherapy, activate CD4 + and CD8 + T cells, and ultimately suppress tumor growth. As a potential oxidative stress-responsive immune checkpoint in cancer, 41BBL is able to increase ROS level in cells. Interestingly, Nfe2l1 can up-regulate ROS level by facilitating the 41BBL expression, strengthen tumor immune response, and ultimately suppress tumor growth [36] . We speculate that the tumor-promoting effect of low-dose of taurine may be achieved by down-regulating Nfe2l1 expression, causing excess ROS, and ultimately inducing immune escape. Our results showed that low dose of taurine (25 mg/kg) can significantly increase PD-1 expression on CD4 + and CD8 + T cells, while low expression of PD-1 appeared in high dose of taurine (200 mg/kg) ( Fig. 1 H). Therefore, taurine might influence tumor immune response through the Nfe2l1-ROS-PD-1 axis in immune-competent mice.

However, in lung cancer nude mice model, we identified 4 DEGs including Ace , Plac8 , Gbp4 and Nod1 between model and taurine group, which were closely related to inflammation in cancers ( Fig. 6 D). Specifically, Ace can produce anti-inflammatory effect in the renin angiotensin system by activating Ace2 / Ang-(1 – 7) / Mas axis [42] . Gbp4 , up-regulated in malignant lung adenocarcinoma, is an important inflammasome adaptor for producing prostaglandin and inducing the clearance of Salmonella typhimurium via neutrophils [41] . Plac8 is a tumor suppressor participating in the proliferation, apoptosis and autophagy of cancer cells [43] . Nod1 , an innate immune sensor involving in anti-inflammation, can suppress tumor growth and strengthen response to chemotherapy by inhibition of SRC-MAPK pathway [44] . In our result, the 4 DEGs were significantly up-regulated in taurine-treated nude mice. Consistent with our findings, the 4 DEGs are down-regulated in lung tumors compared with normal lung tissues ( Supplementary Fig. S23 ). Therefore, taurine might exert anti-tumor effects by inhibiting NF-κB-mediated inflammatory responses in immune-deficient mice.

Functional beverages are drinks available in our daily lives that contain taurine [38] . Given the varying concentrations of taurine found in functional beverages, we assessed the effects of a popular functional drink available on the market. Intriguingly, consumption of the taurine beverage also had opposite effects on tumor growth in C57 and nude mice ( Fig. 5 D-E). Therefore, lung cancer patients, especially young patients, should be conscious of potential effects of taurine-containing drinks. However, with the decline of immune function, the tumor-promoting effect of low-dose taurine mediated by Nfe2l1 is lost. Conversely, taurine might exert anti-tumor effects by inhibiting NF-κB-mediated inflammatory responses. Similarly, in ageing, taurine also contributes to delay ageing and increase longevity in humans by reducing cellular senescence, protecting against telomerase deficiency, restoring mitochondrial function, decreasing DNA damage, and attenuating inflammation [49] . Based on the above findings, taurine or taurine-containing drinks might be more suitable for older or immune deficient patients. In addition, we have also focused on therapeutic strategies for the promoting effects of taurine at low doses on lung tumor growth. Bile acids, particularly cholic acid, ursodeoxycholic acid, and chenodeoxycholic acid, can act as taurine scavengers by forming conjugates with taurine [39] , [40] . Combined with our findings ( Fig. 5 F-G), bile acids could potentially serve as effective agents for scavenging taurine in treatment of lung cancer patients. Based on literature research, Based on literature research, we hypothesize that the reversal of the tumor-promoting effects of low-dose taurine by bile acids may be related to their regulation of immune pathways [50] , [51] .

In addition to our first discovery of taurine's dual role in lung cancer progression, taurine is also reported to inhibit ferroptosis mediated by the crosstalk between tumor cells and tumor-associated macrophages in prostate cancer [52] . Besides, studies have also found the use of taurine in liver cancer, pancreatic cancer and gastric cancer [53] . Especially in gastric cancer, taurine has opposite effects on tumors in immunodeficient and immunocompetent mice. Mechanism study shows that tumor cells outcompete CD8 + T cells for taurine by overexpressing SLC6A6, which activates multiple immune checkpoint genes, leading to T cell death and dysfunction, thereby promoting tumor progression [53] . Then taurine supplementation at a dose of 40 mg/kg via intratumoral injection can rejuvenate exhausted CD8 + T cells and enhance the efficacy of cancer therapies. Likewise, our results found taurine at the dose higher than 100 mg/kg by intraperitoneal injection actively inhibited lung cancer growth with up-regulated PD-1 levels on CD4 + and CD8 + T cells ( Fig. 1 H). Taurine is known to be absorbed primarily in the intestine, with only a small portion entering the bloodstream. As the dosage increases, more taurine enters the tumor tissue through the bloodstream. Additionally, tumor cells have a stronger ability to uptake taurine compared to CD8 + T cells [53] . We hypothesize that compared to intratumoral injection, a high dose of taurine by intraperitoneal injection is required to restore the immune activity of CD8 + T cells and exert anti-tumor effects. Therefore, combining our findings with reported studies, the inhibitory effect of taurine on tumors may depend on the concentration of taurine within the tumor.

This study is the first to document that low-dose taurine significantly promotes lung tumor growth in immune e-competent mice, an effect that diminishes as the taurine dose increases. Mechanistically, taurine’s dual role in lung cancer progression may be closely related to its influence on tumor-immune microenvironment through the Nfe2l1-ROS-PD-1 axis ( Fig. 8 ). In immune-competent mice, a low dose of taurine may promote lung cancer progression by down-regulating Nfe2l1 expression, elevating ROS, impairing immune cell function, particularly that of T cells, and ultimately facilitating tumor immune escape. And a high dose of taurine may inhibit lung cancer progression by up-regulating Nfe2l1 expression, inducing a significant accumulation of ROS, activating immune cell function, and ultimately preventing tumor immune escape. However, in nude mice with T cell deficiencies, the decline in immune function leads to the loss of Nfe2l1′s anti-tumor effects. In contrast, taurine may inhibit lung cancer progression by suppressing NF-κB-mediated inflammatory responses rather than influencing Nfe2l1 function in nude mice. Fig. 8 The potential mechanism of taurine’s dual role in lung cancer progression.

The potential mechanism of taurine’s dual role in lung cancer progression.

Despite the significant findings, this study has several limitations. Firstly, our research is a preliminary observational and mechanistic study that identifies specific phenomena and potential mechanisms of taurine in relation to lung tumors. To better understand the conditions and precautions for taurine use in daily life and among clinical patients, further in-depth studies with larger sample sizes, clinical patient samples, and advanced molecular biology techniques are required. Advanced techniques such as spatial transcriptomics will be applied to further isolate and specifically detect tumor cells and tumor-infiltrating immune cells from lung cancer patient samples. Meanwhile, the study primarily focused on the dosage effects of taurine, but did not extensively investigate the long-term impact of taurine supplementation. Additionally, while the study suggests the potential use of bile acids as taurine scavengers, their efficacy and safety in clinical applications need to be thoroughly evaluated. Future research should address these limitations to provide a more comprehensive understanding of taurine's role in lung cancer progression.
sections.conclusion: Our results showed that taurine holds promise as a potential biomarker for lung cancer progression, capable of predicting both poor prognosis and its inapplicability for specific lung cancer patients. Lung cancer patients, especially young patients, should be conscious of potential effects of taurine-containing drinks. Taurine or taurine-containing drinks might be more suitable for older or immune deficient patients. Our finds help fully understand the role and mechanism of taurine on lung cancer progression and provide a scientific basis for better clinical application of taurine and its products.
